text: पृथ्वी दिवस हर साल 22 अप्रैल को मनाया जाता है। उस दिन दुनिया भर में लोग पेड़ लगाते हैं, समुद्र-तट और पार्क साफ़ करते हैं, रैलियाँ निकालते हैं और [[pollution|प्रदूषण]] और [[@climate-change|जलवायु परिवर्तन]] जैसी समस्याओं के बारे में सीखते हैं। स्कूलों में अक्सर ख़ास पाठ, पोस्टर प्रतियोगिताएँ और सफ़ाई अभियान होते हैं। कुछ परिवार एक घंटे के लिए बत्तियाँ बुझा देते हैं, या गाड़ी की जगह साइकिल चलाते हैं।

sec.t:
1960 के दशक के आख़िर तक बहुत-से अमेरिकी प्रदूषण को लेकर परेशान थे। कारख़ाने नदियों में कचरा उड़ेलते थे, गाड़ियाँ सीसे वाला पेट्रोल जलाती थीं, और [[pesticide|कीटनाशक]] चिड़ियों को मार रहे थे। 1962 में रेचल कार्सन नाम की एक वैज्ञानिक ने *साइलेंट स्प्रिंग* लिखी थी। यह किताब ख़ूब बिकी और इसमें कीटनाशकों से होने वाले नुकसान की चेतावनी दी गई थी।

फिर 1969 की शुरुआत में कैलिफ़ोर्निया के सांता बारबरा के तट के पास एक तेल का कुआँ फट गया। लाखों लीटर तेल समुद्र और समुद्र-तटों पर फैल गया, और समुद्री पक्षी और सील उसमें लिपट गए। कुछ महीने बाद ओहायो की कायाहोगा नदी में, जो तेल वाले कचरे से अटी पड़ी थी, आग लग गई। इसमें पहले भी आग लग चुकी थी, पर इस बार यह ख़बर पूरे देश में फैल गई। जिन लोगों ने कभी प्रकृति के बारे में ज़्यादा नहीं सोचा था, वे भी पूछने लगे कि उनकी अपनी नदियों और हवा को आख़िर हो क्या रहा है।

1990 में, अपनी 20वीं सालगिरह पर, पृथ्वी दिवस दुनिया भर में फैल गया, और लगभग 140 देशों के करीब 20 करोड़ लोगों ने हिस्सा लिया। इसने सरकारों को 1992 में रियो डी जनेरो में हुए बड़े पृथ्वी सम्मेलन की ओर बढ़ने में मदद की।

पृथ्वी दिवस 2016 पर लगभग 175 देशों के नेता न्यूयॉर्क में संयुक्त राष्ट्र में जलवायु परिवर्तन पर पेरिस समझौते पर दस्तख़त करने के लिए इकट्ठा हुए। संयुक्त राष्ट्र अब 22 अप्रैल को अंतरराष्ट्रीय धरती माता दिवस कहता है। हर साल आयोजक एक विषय चुनते हैं, जैसे पेड़ लगाना, [[@plastic-made|प्लास्टिक]] घटाना या साफ़ ऊर्जा अपनाना, ताकि हर जगह के समूह एक ही समय पर एक ही समस्या पर काम कर सकें।

भारत में स्कूल और शहर पेड़ लगाकर, सफ़ाई अभियान चलाकर और भाषणों से पृथ्वी दिवस मनाते हैं। प्रकृति को बचाने का भारत का अपना भी लंबा इतिहास है। 1970 के दशक में, आज के उत्तराखंड में, [[@chipko|चिपको आंदोलन]] की गाँव की औरतें पेड़ों से लिपट गईं ताकि उन्हें काटा न जा सके।

भारत के बहुत-से स्कूल 5 जून के विश्व पर्यावरण दिवस पर, जिसे संयुक्त राष्ट्र ने शुरू किया, और भी ज़्यादा जोश दिखाते हैं। दोनों दिनों के मक़सद मिलते-जुलते हैं, और कुछ स्कूल दोनों मनाते हैं।

text: In summer, land heats up much faster than the sea. Hot air over the land rises.
Cooler, wet air from the ocean rushes in to take its place, bringing clouds and rain. That's the monsoon.
In winter, it flips: the land is cooler, so dry winds blow from land to sea.

quiz.prompt: Mumbai gets drenched every monsoon, but Pune, only about 150 km inland, gets much less rain. Why?

options.t: The Western Ghats make the clouds drop most of their rain first
Pune is closer to a desert
Monsoon clouds avoid big cities

quiz.reveal: Wet winds from the Arabian Sea hit the Western Ghats and are forced to rise. Rising air cools, so the clouds drop heavy rain on the coast and the hills. By the time the air crosses to Pune, much of its water is gone. This drier side is called a rain shadow.

myth: The word monsoon just means heavy rain.

A monsoon is a seasonal change in the direction of the wind. India has two. The summer monsoon brings rain from the south-west to most of the country, and the winter or north-east monsoon brings rain to Tamil Nadu from about October to December.

sec.t:
If you've been to a beach on a sunny afternoon, you may have felt a cool breeze blowing in from the water. The monsoon is the same idea, on the scale of a whole continent and a whole season.

By May, the plains of north India and the high Tibetan Plateau are baking. Air over them rises, leaving low pressure behind. Over the Indian Ocean, the air is cooler and heavier. So moist winds start flowing north-east across the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal. They carry enormous amounts of water evaporated from warm seas. The Himalayas act as a wall, holding the wet air over India.

The [[@imd|India Meteorological Department]] declares the monsoon's arrival in [[@kerala|Kerala]], usually around 1 June. From there, one branch sweeps up the west coast, and another curls in from the Bay of Bengal over the Northeast. Normally they cover the whole country by about 8 July. The rains usually reach [[@mumbai|Mumbai]] around 11 June and Delhi near the end of June, and people in both cities follow the monsoon's progress like the score in a cricket match.

The [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]] force the wet winds upward, so the coast gets drenched while places just inland stay much drier. In Meghalaya, winds from the Bay of Bengal funnel into the Khasi Hills, and villages like Mawsynram get more than 11 metres of rain in a typical year.

The India Meteorological Department forecasts the monsoon using [[@ocean-and-climate|ocean temperatures]], winds and [[@supercomputers|computer models]]. Forecasts use [[@chance-weather|probability]].

Monsoon forecasting led to a big discovery. In the 1920s, Gilbert Walker, the head of the department, searched old weather records for clues. He found a giant see-saw in air pressure between the Indian and Pacific Oceans, which he called the [[@el-nino|Southern Oscillation]]. Today we know it is linked to El Niño, a warming of the Pacific that often weakens India's rains.

Sailors used these seasonal winds for thousands of years to cross the Arabian Sea.

Ships from Arabia, Egypt and Rome sailed to [[@kochi|Kerala's ports]] with the summer winds and went home when the winds reversed in winter. The word "monsoon" itself came to English from the Arabic word for season, by way of Portuguese sailors. India isn't the only place with a monsoon. [[@grand-canyon-state|Arizona]] in the USA has a summer monsoon too, with sudden storms rolling over the desert.

text: Dark matter is the name scientists give to something they cannot see but whose pull they can measure. [[galaxy|Galaxies]] spin too fast. Clusters of galaxies hold together too tightly. Light from distant galaxies bends too much as it passes by. In every case, there is far more [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] than the visible stars and gas can explain.

So [[astronomer|astronomers]] think the universe is full of an invisible kind of matter, about five times more than ordinary matter. It does not shine, reflect light or block it. It only pulls. What it is made of remains one of the biggest unsolved questions in science.

st.reveal: For every kilogram of ordinary matter, the stuff of stars and people, there seem to be more than 5 kilograms of dark matter. We can only detect it through its gravity.

sec.t:
In 1933, a Swiss astronomer in California, Fritz Zwicky, studied a huge group of galaxies called the Coma Cluster. The galaxies were moving so fast that the cluster should have flown apart long ago. Something unseen had to be holding it together. He called it dunkle Materie, German for dark matter.

Few people took him seriously at first. Zwicky was famous for wild ideas and a prickly temper, and it took about 40 years for the evidence to catch up.

[[@einstein|Einstein]] showed that mass bends space, so light passing a heavy object curves, like a ball rolling past a dip in a trampoline. This is called gravitational lensing. Galaxy clusters act as giant lenses, stretching the light of galaxies behind them into arcs.

By measuring the bending, astronomers can map where the mass is. In a pair of colliding galaxy clusters known as the Bullet Cluster, the hot gas, which holds most of the ordinary matter, piled up in the middle. But the lensing showed most of the mass had passed straight through, on either side. Dark matter, it seems, hardly bumps into anything, not even itself.

Most physicists think dark matter is some kind of particle not yet discovered. If so, huge numbers of them may be passing through your body right now, without a trace. To catch one, scientists have built detectors filled with tonnes of liquid xenon, a heavy gas cooled into a liquid, deep underground, where rock blocks other particles. One sits about 1.5 km below the ground in an old gold mine in South Dakota, USA.

So far, none has found a clear signal, even after years of watching. Some scientists suspect the particles are even lighter or stranger than expected. A smaller group argues there is no dark matter at all, and that gravity behaves differently over enormous distances.

Measurements from the European Planck space telescope suggest the universe is about 5% ordinary matter, about 27% dark matter, and about 68% something even stranger. That last part, called [[@mystery-dark-energy|dark energy]], seems to be pushing the universe apart faster and faster. Put together, the planets, stars and everything you have ever touched are a small sprinkle on top of a universe we barely understand.

text: The electricity in your wall socket is strong and restless. In India it pushes at about 230 volts and flips direction 50 times a second. In the USA it's about 120 volts, flipping 60 times a second. This is called alternating current.

A phone's [[@batteries-phones|battery]] wants something very different: about 4 volts, flowing steadily in one direction, known as direct current. A charger is the go-between. It lowers the voltage, straightens the back-and-forth flow into a one-way stream, smooths it out and keeps it steady. Then a small chip inside the phone decides how fast to fill the battery, so it doesn't overheat.

st.reveal: The charger doesn't store anything. It takes mains electricity and changes it into the steady, low-voltage direct current a lithium-ion battery needs. A chip inside the phone then decides how fast the battery actually fills.

sec.t:
Older chargers, the kind that felt like a brick, used a simple transformer. Inside were two coils of copper wire wrapped around an iron core.

[[@electricity-home|Mains electricity]] flowing through the first coil makes a changing magnetic field. That field passes through the iron and creates a smaller voltage in the second coil, which has fewer turns of wire. It's [[@magnets-how|magnets]] doing the work. Then a set of one-way electronic valves called diodes turned the alternating current into direct current.

These chargers were reliable, but they had to be heavy. At 50 or 60 flips a second, a transformer needs a lot of iron and copper to do its job, and it wastes energy as heat.

When you plug in a modern phone, it and the charger hold a quick conversation through the cable. The phone says how much power it can take. The charger replies with what it can offer. Basic USB gives 5 volts. Fast-charging systems such as USB Power Delivery can step up to 9, 15 or 20 volts, so more energy flows without needing a thicker wire.

Charging usually goes fastest at first. Once the battery reaches about 80%, the phone slows down to protect it, a bit like filling a glass quickly and then pouring gently near the top.

Wireless chargers use the same magnetic idea as the old transformer, but with one coil in the pad and the other in the phone. They're handy but waste more energy as heat, which is why they feel warm. The phone also has to sit in just the right spot, because the two coils must line up closely for the magnetic field to pass between them.

For years, every brand seemed to have its own plug. People ended up with drawers full of cables that fit nothing. The European Union decided that, from the end of 2024, new phones sold there must use USB-C. India announced plans to follow, and other countries are moving the same way. The aim is to cut costs and reduce [[@e-waste|e-waste]], the mountains of old gadgets thrown away every year.

A good charger left in the socket with no phone attached draws only a tiny amount of power. Cheap, badly made chargers are another matter. They can overheat or give shocks, so it's safest to use ones with proper safety marks and never to charge a phone under a pillow.

text: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water. The iron [[atom|atoms]] give up some of their [[electron|electrons]] to oxygen, a kind of reaction called [[oxidation|oxidation]]. The result is a new substance, iron oxide, mixed with water. That's the flaky, reddish-brown crust we call rust.
Iron needs both oxygen and water to rust. A nail kept completely dry, or completely sealed under oil, barely changes. Leave it out in damp air, and rust appears within days.

Unlike many other metals, iron has a problem. Its rust is crumbly and flakes away, which exposes fresh iron underneath to more air and water. So once rusting starts, it can keep eating deeper and deeper until a strong iron bar crumbles.

st.prompt: You leave three iron nails for a week, one in a dry jar, one in tap water and one in salty water. Which rusts most?

options.t: The one in salty water
The one in the dry jar
They all rust the same amount

st.reveal: Rust needs both water and oxygen, so the dry nail barely changes. Salt dissolved in water helps electric charges move more easily, which speeds up the reaction. That's why cars, bridges and railings near the sea rust much faster.

sec.t:
Rust is really a tiny electrical process. Charges have to move through the water on the iron's surface. Pure water doesn't carry charge very well, but salty water does. That's why iron rusts much faster near the sea.

In coastal cities like Mumbai, Chennai and Miami, railings, cars and old buildings rust quickly in the salty, damp air. In places with cold winters, such as Chicago or Toronto, salt spread on icy roads speeds up rust on cars. Ships face the hardest test of all, sitting in salt water for years. That's why their steel hulls need thick paint and regular care to stay afloat, as you can read in [[@floating-ships|floating ships]].

The simplest way is to keep water and air away from the iron. Paint, oil and grease all form a barrier. The [[@eiffel-tower|Eiffel Tower]] in Paris is repainted roughly every seven years to protect its iron.

Another way is galvanising, coating steel with a thin layer of zinc. Zinc reacts with air first and protects the iron below, even if the coating gets scratched. Many buckets, roofing sheets and lamp posts are galvanised. You can often spot the zinc as a dull grey surface with a faint pattern, like frost on a window.

Stainless steel contains chromium, at least about 10% of the mix. The chromium forms a thin, invisible layer on the surface that seals the steel. That's why steel tiffins, kitchen sinks and spoons stay shiny for years.

{{story:statue-liberty}}

In the Qutub complex in [[@delhi|Delhi]] stands [[@mystery-iron-pillar|an iron pillar]] more than 7 metres tall. It carries an [[inscription|inscription]] in Sanskrit, and it is usually dated to the reign of Chandragupta II in the [[@gupta-golden-age|Gupta period]], around 400 CE. Despite standing in the open for about 1,600 years, it shows very little rust.

Scientists, including R. Balasubramaniam of IIT Kanpur, studied it closely. They found the iron contains an unusually high amount of phosphorus and very little sulphur. Over time, this helped a thin, tightly sticking protective layer form on the surface. Delhi's fairly dry [[climate|climate]] helps too.

The red colour of [[@mars-colonies|Mars]] comes from iron oxide in its rocks and dust. Billions of years ago, scientists think, the planet had liquid water, which may have helped rust its iron-rich surface.

Not every metal "rusts" the way iron does. Copper turns green over time, which is why the [[@statue-liberty|Statue of Liberty]] in New York, made of thin copper sheets, is pale green instead of the shiny brown it was in 1886. That green layer, called a [[patina|patina]], protects the copper underneath, unlike iron's flaky rust.

sec.t:
चोल राजाओं ने पत्थर के विशाल मंदिर बनवाए, जैसे तंजावुर का [[@india-wonder-brihadeeswara|बृहदीश्वर मंदिर]], जिसके बारे में [[@architecture-temples|भारत के विशाल मंदिर कैसे बने?]] में पढ़ सकते हो। मंदिर की मुख्य पत्थर की मूर्ति गर्भगृह में अपनी जगह पर स्थिर रहती है।

पर त्योहारों पर देवताओं को शोभायात्रा में गलियों से घुमाया जाता था, रथों पर बिठाकर और कंधों पर उठाकर। इसके लिए मंदिरों को ऐसी मूर्तियाँ चाहिए थीं जो सुंदर हों, मज़बूत हों और इतनी हल्की हों कि उठाई जा सकें। धातु इसके लिए एकदम सही थी। बहुत-सी चोल काँसा मूर्तियों के आधार में कड़े या छेद हैं, जिनमें उठाने के लिए डंडे फँसाए जा सकते थे।

सबसे मशहूर चोल काँसा मूर्ति है नटराज, यानी नृत्य के स्वामी शिव। वे लपटों के घेरे के अंदर नाच रहे हैं, एक पैर उठा हुआ है, और उनकी जटाएँ दोनों तरफ़ उड़ रही हैं। एक हाथ में वे छोटा-सा डमरू लिए हैं, जिसकी थाप सृष्टि की रचना का प्रतीक है। दूसरे हाथ में आग है, जो विनाश का प्रतीक है। उनके पैर के नीचे एक छोटी आकृति है, जो अज्ञान को दर्शाती है।

यह मुद्रा [[@indian-classical-dance|शास्त्रीय नृत्य]] की चालों से मेल खाती है, और [[@bharatanatyam|भरतनाट्यम]] के नर्तक आज भी इनमें से कुछ मुद्राएँ अपनाते हैं। चोल मूर्तिकारों ने पार्वती, विष्णु, लक्ष्मी, संतों और कवियों की कोमल मूर्तियाँ भी बनाईं।

तमिलनाडु में कुंभकोणम के पास बसे कस्बे स्वामीमलै में कारीगरों के परिवार आज भी पुराने ढंग से काँसे की मूर्तियाँ ढालते हैं। मिट्टी आज भी वहीं की नदियों की तली से आती है, और साँचे आज भी हाथ से तोड़े जाते हैं। "स्वामीमलै ब्रॉन्ज़ आइकन्स" को अब भौगोलिक संकेत (जीआई) मिला हुआ है, यानी एक कानूनी ठप्पा जो यह नाम सिर्फ़ वहाँ पारंपरिक ढंग से बनी मूर्तियों के लिए सुरक्षित रखता है।

छोटी मूर्ति में कई दिन लगते हैं। बड़ी मूर्ति में, मोम की पहली आकृति से आख़िरी चमक तक, कई महीने लग सकते हैं।

चोल काँसा मूर्तियाँ इतनी सुंदर और कीमती हैं कि कुछ को मंदिरों से चुराकर चोरी-छिपे विदेश भेज दिया गया। हाल के बरसों में ऑस्ट्रेलिया और अमेरिका समेत कई देशों के संग्रहालयों और संग्रह करने वालों ने चोरी की मूर्तियाँ भारत को लौटाई हैं, जब जाँच करने वालों ने साबित कर दिया कि वे कहाँ से आई थीं।

जिन गाँवों से वे खोई थीं, उनके लिए ये सिर्फ़ कला के नमूने नहीं हैं। ये वे देवता हैं जो कभी एक मंदिर और उसके लोगों के थे, जिन्हें त्योहारों पर गलियों से घुमाया जाता था, ठीक वैसे ही जैसा [[@cholas|चोलों]] ने एक हज़ार साल पहले सोचा था।

सिम्फ़नी ऑर्केस्ट्रा के कलाकार अपने-अपने वाद्यों की टोलियों में बैठते हैं। सबसे बड़ी टोली तार वाद्यों की है: वायलिन, वियोला, चेलो और डबल बेस। ये आम तौर पर सबसे आगे, संचालक के चारों ओर अर्धचंद्र में बैठते हैं।

इनके पीछे वुडविंड बैठते हैं, जैसे [[@flutes|बाँसुरी]], ओबो, क्लैरिनेट और बैसून। उनसे पीछे ब्रास: ट्रम्पेट, हॉर्न, ट्रॉम्बोन और ट्यूबा। सबसे पीछे ताल-वाद्य होते हैं, जिनमें बड़े टिंपनी ढोल, झाँझ और ज़ाइलोफ़ोन शामिल हैं। ज़ोरदार वाद्य दूर बैठते हैं, ताकि धीमे तार वाद्यों की आवाज़ न दबा दें।

कॉन्सर्ट शुरू होने से पहले एक अजीब-सा घुमड़ता शोर सुनाई देता है। यह ऑर्केस्ट्रा सुर मिला रहा होता है। ओबो एक अकेला सुर बजाता है, A, और सब अपने वाद्य उसी से मिला लेते हैं। तार वाद्य बजाने वाले खूँटियाँ घुमाते हैं। फूँक वाले वाद्यों के कलाकार अपने वाद्य के हिस्से अंदर-बाहर सरकाते हैं, कुछ वैसे ही जैसे शास्त्रीय संगीत की महफ़िल से पहले तानपूरा और तबला मिलाए जाते हैं।

ओबो ही क्यों? उसकी आवाज़ चमकीली है और सबको चीरकर निकलती है, और उसका [[pitch|सुर]] स्थिर रहता है। बहुत-से ऑर्केस्ट्रा ऐसे A पर सुर मिलाते हैं जिसकी [[frequency|आवृत्ति]] 440 है, यानी जो एक सेकंड में 440 बार [[vibration|कंपन]] करता है, हालाँकि कुछ थोड़ा ऊँचा पसंद करते हैं।

हर कलाकार बस अपना हिस्सा पढ़ता है। संचालक पूरा स्कोर पढ़ता है, जिसमें हर वाद्य का हिस्सा एक ही पन्ने पर एक के ऊपर एक लिखा होता है, किसी विशाल रेलवे समय-सारणी की तरह। स्कोर के एक पन्ने पर संगीत की बीस से ज़्यादा पंक्तियाँ हो सकती हैं। यह कैसे लिखा जाता है, यह तुम [[@music-notes|स्वरलिपि]] में जान सकते हो।

रिहर्सल में संचालक ट्रम्पेट वालों से धीमा बजाने को कह सकता है, या चेलो वालों से किसी टुकड़े को खींचकर लंबा करने को। दो संचालक एक ही रचना की अगुआई करें, तो वह काफ़ी अलग सुनाई दे सकती है। कुछ संचालक नन्ही, सटीक हरकतों के लिए मशहूर हैं। दूसरे उछलते, झुकते और बाँहें लहराते हैं, और दोनों तरीके काम कर सकते हैं।

1842 में बना न्यूयॉर्क फ़िलहार्मोनिक अमेरिका का सबसे पुराना ऑर्केस्ट्रा है। न्यूयॉर्क का कार्नेगी हॉल 1891 में खुला, और उसकी पहली रात रूसी संगीतकार चाइकोव्स्की ने संचालन किया।

भारत की अपनी कहानी है। [[@mumbai|मुंबई]] में जन्मे संचालक ज़ुबिन मेहता ने दशकों तक न्यूयॉर्क फ़िलहार्मोनिक और इज़राइल फ़िलहार्मोनिक की अगुआई की। 2006 में मुंबई में सिम्फ़नी ऑर्केस्ट्रा ऑफ़ इंडिया बना। बहुत-से भारतीय [[@film-songs|फ़िल्मी गानों]] के पीछे भी ऑर्केस्ट्रा बजते हैं, और [[@ar-rahman|ए. आर. रहमान]] जैसे संगीतकारों ने अपनी फ़िल्मों के संगीत के लिए तार वाद्यों की बड़ी मंडलियों के साथ रिकॉर्डिंग की है।

text: ग्रैफ़िटी का मतलब है दीवारों और दूसरी सार्वजनिक जगहों पर लिखी या बनाई गई चीज़ें। इनमें से कुछ, जैसे किसी दुकान के शटर पर जल्दबाज़ी में स्प्रे किए टैग, आमतौर पर तोड़फोड़ माने जाते हैं। दूसरे काम, ख़ासकर इजाज़त लेकर बनाए गए बड़े, हुनर भरे [[mural|भित्तिचित्र]], बड़े पैमाने पर कला माने जाते हैं। बहुत से शहर अब ख़ुद कलाकारों को अपनी दीवारें सजाने बुलाते हैं।

तो क्या ग्रैफ़िटी कला है? यह इस पर निर्भर है कि तुम किससे पूछ रहे हो, और कौन सी कृति की बात हो रही है। किसी और की संपत्ति पर बिना इजाज़त रंग चलाना लगभग हर जगह क़ानून के ख़िलाफ़ है, चाहे वह दिखे कैसा भी। पर कुछ ग्रैफ़िटी लिखने वाले दुनिया भर में मशहूर कलाकार बन गए हैं, और उनका काम आज संग्रहालयों में टँगा है।

sec.t:
आधुनिक ग्रैफ़िटी 1960 के दशक के आख़िर और 1970 के दशक में फ़िलाडेल्फ़िया और [[@new-york|न्यूयॉर्क]] में पनपी। नौजवान दीवारों और सबवे ट्रेनों पर अपने उपनाम लिखने लगे, जिन्हें टैग कहा गया। जल्दी ही टैग बढ़कर विशाल, रंगीन "पीस" बन गए, जिनमें गुब्बारे जैसे अक्षर, तीर और कार्टून पात्र होते थे।

ग्रैफ़िटी [[@hip-hop|हिप-हॉप]] संस्कृति के चार हिस्सों में से एक बन गई, डीजे करने, रैप करने और ब्रेकडांस के साथ। पर बहुत से न्यूयॉर्कवासियों को यह बेक़ाबू शहर की निशानी लगती थी। 1980 के दशक में सबवे ने ट्रेनों से ग्रैफ़िटी हटाना शुरू किया, ताकि कोई भी रंगी हुई ट्रेन सेवा में न रहे।

कुछ ग्रैफ़िटी कलाकार गैलरियों में अपना काम दिखाने लगे। 1980 के दशक में कीथ हैरिंग न्यूयॉर्क के सबवे स्टेशनों पर ख़ाली पड़े [[@advertising|विज्ञापन]] बोर्डों पर चॉक से आकृतियाँ बनाते थे। फिर वे अपने नाचते, चमकते कार्टूनी लोगों के लिए दुनिया भर में मशहूर हो गए।

ब्रिटेन में [[@banksy|बैंक्सी]] नाम से जाने जाने वाले एक कलाकार ने 1990 के दशक में ब्रिस्टल की दीवारों पर स्टेंसिल से चुटीली तस्वीरें बनानी शुरू कीं। सार्वजनिक रूप से कोई नहीं जानता कि बैंक्सी कौन है। उनकी कृतियाँ करोड़ों में बिकती हैं, और लोग कभी-कभी उन्हें बेचने के लिए दीवार का पूरा हिस्सा ही काट ले जाते हैं। 2018 में उनकी एक तस्वीर, *गर्ल विद बलून*, लंदन की एक नीलामी के ठीक बाद ख़ुद ही आधी कतर गई।

भित्तिचित्र दमदार संदेश दे सकते हैं। 1920 के दशक में [[@mexico|मेक्सिको]] में [[@frida-kahlo|फ़्रीडा काहलो]] के पति डिएगो रिवेरा जैसे चित्रकारों ने सरकारी इमारतों को मेक्सिको के इतिहास वाले भित्तिचित्रों से ढक दिया, ताकि कला सिर्फ़ अमीरों की न रहे, हर कोई उसे देख सके।

जब बर्लिन की दीवार शहर को बाँटती थी, तब कलाकार उसके पश्चिमी हिस्से पर चित्र बनाते थे। 1989 में दीवार गिरने के बाद कई देशों के कलाकारों ने बची हुई दीवार के लगभग 1.3 किलोमीटर हिस्से को रंग दिया। इसे ईस्ट साइड गैलरी कहते हैं, और आज यह बर्लिन की सबसे ज़्यादा देखी जाने वाली जगहों में से है।

भारत में रंगी हुई दीवारों का लंबा इतिहास है, गाँव के घरों से लेकर फ़िल्मी पोस्टरों तक। 2010 के दशक से समारोह कलाकारों को शहरों में बड़े-बड़े भित्तिचित्र बनाने बुलाने लगे। [[@delhi|दिल्ली]] में लोधी आर्ट डिस्ट्रिक्ट में एक सरकारी आवासीय कॉलोनी की दीवारों पर दर्जनों विशाल भित्तिचित्र हैं। [[@mumbai|मुंबई]] में कलाकारों ने ससून डॉक के गोदामों और बांद्रा की दीवारों को रंगा है।

हर भित्तिचित्र हर किसी को पसंद नहीं आता, और कुछ रहने वालों का कहना है कि उनसे पहले पूछा ही नहीं गया। क़ानूनी स्ट्रीट आर्ट भी वही सवाल खड़ा करती है जो इस बहस के बीच में है: जिन दीवारों को सब बाँटते हैं, उन पर क्या बने, यह तय करने का हक़ किसका है?

text: Science suggests that being kind is often good for the person doing it, as well as for the person receiving it. Studies have found that people who help others, give gifts or volunteer tend to report feeling happier, more connected and less [[@stress|stressed]].

The effects are usually modest, not magic, and researchers are still working out how much kindness itself causes these benefits. But the pattern turns up again and again, in different countries and age groups. Being kind also builds [[@friendship|friendships]], and strong relationships are one of the best-known links to health and [[@happiness|happiness]].

Experiments show that toddlers often help others before they can say much, without any reward. Families and culture shape how kindness grows, but the urge to help seems to start early.

sec.t:
In a famous 2008 study in Canada, psychologists Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton gave people an envelope of money in the morning. Some were told to spend it on themselves, others on a gift for someone else or a donation. By evening, the people who had spent on others reported feeling happier.

The amounts were small, five or twenty dollars, and the amount did not seem to matter much. What mattered was who it was spent on. Later studies found similar patterns in countries as different as Uganda, India and Canada.

Psychologists Felix Warneken and Michael Tomasello tested whether very young children help without being asked. An adult would "accidentally" drop a pen or struggle to open a cupboard with full hands. Many toddlers aged about 18 months toddled over and helped, even with no praise or reward. Young chimpanzees helped in some tests too.

This suggests the urge to help starts early in life. Families, friends and culture then shape it. Children learn when, how and whom to help by watching others.

Humans are not the only kind creatures. In a 2011 experiment in the United States, rats learned how to open a small cage to free a trapped companion. They did this even when they could have eaten a pile of chocolate chips alone instead. Many rats shared the chocolate afterwards. Elephants, chimpanzees and some birds also help each other in ways scientists are still studying.

Many cultures have long taught this. Ideas such as *seva*, selfless service, and *daya*, compassion, appear across Indian traditions, and similar teachings are found in religions and [[philosophy|philosophies]] worldwide.

Kindness does not have to be big. Holding a door, saying thank you, including someone who is left out, or listening when a friend is upset all count. Researchers have found that people often underestimate how much a small kind act means to the person receiving it.

There is one caution. Helping others is good, but nobody should feel they must please everyone all the time or ignore their own feelings. Kindness works best when it includes being kind to yourself, and asking a trusted adult for help when you need it. Our [[@emotions|emotions]] are part of what makes caring for others possible.

text: [[probability|Probability]] is the maths of how likely something is. 0% means impossible, 100% means certain, and everything in between is a maybe.

A "70% chance of rain" means that on days with weather like today's, it rains at your spot about 7 times out of 10. It doesn't tell you how long it will rain or how hard. A 70% day might bring a ten-minute shower. A 40% day might bring a downpour, if it rains at all.
Weather forecasts use [[@coding-maths|computer models]] and lots of past weather to work out these chances.

d.try: Keep a rain diary for a month. Each morning, write down the chance of rain from a weather app or the newspaper, then note at bedtime whether it rained. At the end, look at all the days that said 60% or more. Did it rain on most of them?
myth: If it doesn't rain on a "70% chance" day, the forecast was wrong.
A 70% forecast expects dry weather about 3 times in 10. You can only judge a forecaster over many days, by checking whether their 70% days really are wet about 70% of the time.
facts: rain on about 7 of 10 days like this one
up to about a week, much less certain beyond two weeks

sec.t:
Forecasters don't run their computer model of the [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] just once. Tiny errors in today's measurements can grow into big differences a few days later. So they run the model dozens of times, each with slightly different starting numbers.

If 35 out of 50 runs show rain over your town tomorrow, that is 70%. If almost every run agrees, the forecast is confident. If the runs scatter in all directions, the chance stays close to the middle.

In the 1960s, an American meteorologist named Edward Lorenz found that the atmosphere is so sensitive that forecasts lose their grip after about two weeks. That is why nobody can promise sunshine for a wedding next month.

sec.h: Forecasting rain for a billion people
sec.t:
India's Meteorological Department, set up in 1875, makes forecasts that help farmers decide when to sow seeds before the [[@monsoon|monsoon]]. It predicts when the rains will reach Kerala, usually around the start of June, and how much rain the season will bring.

Those forecasts are probabilities too. A prediction of a "normal" [[monsoon|monsoon]] really means it is the most likely outcome, not a promise. Rain itself starts high above, when tiny droplets in [[@clouds-rain|clouds]] join and grow heavy enough to fall.

Probability is everywhere once you look. A cricket captain calling heads at the toss has a 50% chance of winning it, however lucky the coin feels. A [[@maths-games|board game]] dice lands on six about once in every six throws, over many throws, though it can easily miss six times in a row.

Weather is harder, because the sky is not a coin. The atmosphere is a huge, swirling mixture of air, heat and water, and nobody can measure every part of it. A forecast number is an honest way of saying how much we know, and how much we don't.

A good forecaster is "well calibrated". On all the days they said 30%, it should rain about 30% of the time. Big weather services check this constantly and are usually close.

Some US television weather presenters have been found to forecast rain a little more often than it happens. People grumble more about a surprise soaking than a surprise sunny day. Studies also show that many people misread the number, as the quiz above shows. Learning a little about [[@probability|probability]] means you can read a forecast the way a forecaster does, and pack your umbrella on a 30% day anyway.

text: When you count normally on your fingers, each finger is worth 1, so ten fingers reach 10. In finger [[binary|binary]], each finger is worth double the one before. Your right thumb is 1, then 2, 4, 8 and 16 across the rest of that hand. Your left hand goes on: 32, 64, 128, 256 and 512.

To show a number, you raise the fingers that add up to it. Five is the thumb plus the middle finger, 1 + 4. Twenty is the middle finger plus the little finger, 4 + 16. With all ten fingers up, you get 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 + 64 + 128 + 256 + 512 = 1,023. That's more than a hundred times further than counting the usual way.

st.prompt: In finger binary, your right thumb is worth 1, index finger 2, middle finger 4, ring finger 8 and little finger 16. Which number do you show by raising only your thumb and ring finger?
st.reveal: Add up the raised fingers. The thumb is 1 and the ring finger is 8, so 1 + 8 = 9. Every number from 0 to 31 has exactly one pattern on one hand.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Binary number system.
Leibniz G. W., Explication de l'Arithmétique Binaire (1703).
Ifrah G., The Universal History of Numbers (Wiley, 2000).

d.try: Count from 0 to 31 on one hand in binary. Start with a closed fist for 0. Raise your thumb for 1, then lower it and raise your index finger for 2, then raise both for 3. Keep going, adding 1 each time. When you reach 31, all five fingers are up. Then try spelling your age.
myth: Binary is a special computer language that only programmers can understand.
Binary is just a way of writing numbers using two digits instead of ten. Anyone who can add can learn it. Children often learn finger binary in a few minutes.
facts: Highest number on 10 fingers in binary
up to 12 on one hand, using the thumb on finger joints

sec.t:
Each finger has only two choices: up or down. Think of up as 1 and down as 0. A number written this way, using just 1s and 0s, is called [[@binary-code|binary]].

In our everyday system, each place is worth ten times the one to its right: ones, tens, hundreds. In binary, each place is worth two times the one to its right: ones, twos, fours, eights. Your fingers act as the places. The idea of [[@place-value|place value]] is the same. Only the multiplying number changes, from 10 to 2.

Computers use binary because their tiny switches have just two states, on and off, like a finger up or down. A computer chip contains billions of these switches.

Eight binary digits, or bits, make a byte. One byte can show 256 different patterns, enough to stand for every letter, number and symbol on a keyboard. A photo on a phone might take a few million bytes. Your fingers are a 10-bit computer, slow but always with you.

The German mathematician Gottfried Leibniz wrote about binary in detail in 1703. Much earlier, the Indian scholar Pingala, writing about poetry more than 2,000 years ago, described patterns of long and short [[syllable|syllables]] in a way that matches binary counting.

Indian traditions have their own clever finger counting. Many people count up to 12 on one hand by touching the thumb to each of the three segments on the other four fingers. With the other hand keeping track of each 12, you can reach 60. This may be linked to ancient systems based on 12 and 60, the reason an hour has 60 minutes.

People use joint counting when chanting mantras or counting days. Some merchants once used secret finger signals, hidden under a cloth, to agree prices without others seeing.

Here are some to test yourself. 7 is the thumb, index and middle fingers: 1 + 2 + 4. 10 is the index and ring fingers: 2 + 8. 31 is the whole hand up. To show 100 with both hands, raise the fingers for 64, 32 and 4.

Once you know the pattern, any number up to 1,023 has a shape. It is the same way the numbers inside a [[@computers-how|computer]] work, one bit at a time.

text: In the 1700s, the city of Königsberg in Prussia sat on both banks of the River Pregel, with two islands in the middle. Seven bridges joined the four pieces of land. Locals wondered whether you could walk through the city crossing every bridge exactly once. People tried. Nobody could.

In 1736 the Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler proved it was impossible. His clever idea was to forget the streets, houses and distances, and draw each piece of land as a dot and each bridge as a line. That simple picture launched a whole new branch of maths, now called graph theory. It's the maths behind delivery routes, phone maps and the internet.

st.prompt: In Königsberg, each of the four land areas had an odd number of bridges. What did Euler prove about a walk crossing every bridge exactly once?

options.t: It was impossible, however you tried
It was possible, but only starting on the island
It was possible, but only at night when bridges were empty

st.reveal: Every time you walk through a place, you use one bridge in and one bridge out. So any place you pass through needs an even number of bridges. Only your start and finish can have odd numbers. Königsberg had four odd places, so no route could work.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Königsberg bridge problem and Leonhard Euler.
Mathematical Association of America, Euler's paper on the Königsberg bridges (1736, published 1741).

d.try: Try to draw the "house" shape, a square with a triangle roof and an X across the square, without lifting your pencil or going over a line twice. Count how many lines meet at each corner first. Euler's rule says you must start at a corner with an odd number of lines. Try it both ways and see.
myth: You can only prove something is impossible by trying every possible route.
Euler didn't test a single walk. He found a simple reason, counting bridges at each place, that rules out every route at once. That's the power of a mathematical proof.
facts: a route works only if 0 or 2 places have an odd number of bridges

sec.h: The puzzle of the Sunday walk
sec.t:
Königsberg was a busy trading city on the Baltic Sea. The Pregel river split around an island called Kneiphof, with a second island just downstream. Over the centuries, the townspeople built seven [[@bridges|bridges]] linking the islands and the two riverbanks.

The challenge became a local game. Start anywhere, finish anywhere, but cross each bridge exactly once. No swimming, no boats, no doubling back over a bridge. It sounds like it should be possible with enough patience.

Euler worked in St Petersburg and heard about the puzzle in letters. He noticed something important: the shape of the land didn't matter. Only the connections did. So he imagined each land area as a point and each bridge as a line between points.

Then he thought about any walk. Each time you enter a piece of land by one bridge, you must leave it by another. So every place you pass through uses up bridges in pairs and needs an even number of them. Only the starting place and the finishing place can have an odd number.

In Königsberg, one area had five bridges and the other three had three each. All four were odd. A walk could have at most two odd places, its start and its end, so the walk was impossible. Not difficult. Impossible. That kind of certainty is what [[@logic|logic]] and proof can give you.

{{story:maps-digital}}

Euler's dots-and-lines drawing is called a graph. It isn't the same as the bar charts you draw in school. Here a graph means a network: points, called nodes, joined by lines, called edges.

Graphs turn up everywhere. Cities and roads form one. So do friends on social media, airports and flights, and computers linked by cables. When a phone [[@maps-digital|map app]] finds you the quickest route, it searches a giant graph of roads. Messages crossing the [[@internet-how|internet]] hop between nodes too.

Euler went on to write more maths than almost anyone in history. He kept working even after losing most of his sight, doing huge sums in his head.

In the early 1960s a Chinese mathematician named Kwan Mei-Ko asked a related question. A postman must walk down every street at least once and return home. If he can't avoid repeating some streets, which ones should he repeat to walk the least? It's now called the Chinese postman problem, and councils use versions of it to plan routes for rubbish lorries, snowploughs and street sweepers.

Königsberg was heavily bombed in 1944, near the end of the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]]. Afterwards, the city became part of the Soviet Union and was renamed Kaliningrad. Today it belongs to Russia. Some of Euler's bridges were destroyed and never rebuilt, and others were replaced.

The new layout changed the maths. With the bridges as they are now, only two land areas have an odd number of crossings. So Euler's walk can finally be done, starting at one odd area and ending at the other. And the strangest part? Another famous puzzle uses the same habit of breaking a big problem into simpler pieces, the legendary [[@puzzle-tower-hanoi|Tower of Hanoi]].

text: Partly. Badminton as we know it took shape in the 19th century, among British army officers stationed in India and among wealthy families in England. The officers played a version in Poona, now [[@pune|Pune]], and the game was even called "Poona" for a while.

The name badminton comes from Badminton House, a country estate of the Duke of Beaufort in England, where the game was played in the 1870s. People had been hitting shuttlecocks back and forth with paddles for centuries before either.

st.prompt: A shuttle can fly off the racket at over 400 km/h, yet it lands gently. Why does it slow down so fast?

options.t: Its feathers catch the air and create a lot of drag
It is heavier at the back than the front
The cork absorbs the speed

st.reveal: The feather skirt pushes against the air like a parachute, so drag rises steeply at high speed. The shuttle also always flips to fly cork-first, because the heavy cork is at the front.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, Badminton.
Guinness World Records, Fastest badminton hit in competition (male), 2023.
n.certNote: Historians agree that early rules were drawn up by British officers in India and that the name comes from Badminton House in England. Which place deserves more credit is argued over, and shuttlecock games are much older than both.

d.try: Drop a shuttlecock and a small ball from the same height and watch which lands first. Then drop the shuttle feathers-down. It flips over and falls cork-first every time, because of where its weight sits.
myth: Badminton was invented in India.
British officers in India helped shape the modern rules in the 1860s and 1870s. But people in China, Japan, India, Greece and Europe had played shuttlecock games for many centuries before that.

sec.t:
Games with a feathered shuttle are very old. In [[@china-today|China]], people played jianzi, kicking a weighted shuttle with their feet, for over 2,000 years. In Europe, children played battledore and shuttlecock, keeping a shuttle in the air with small wooden bats.

Similar games were played in India and Japan. What none of these had was a net, a court and a way to score points against an opponent.

A competition shuttle has 16 goose or duck feathers fixed into a rounded cork base. The feathers overlap slightly, like the blades of a fan, which makes the shuttle spin as it flies.

The shape gives it a strange flight. A hard smash leaves the racket at enormous speed, but the feathers create so much [[drag|drag]] that it slows sharply. In 2023, India's Satwiksairaj Rankireddy set a Guinness World Record with a smash measured at 565 km/h. That is faster than a [[@formula-one|Formula One]] car, yet the shuttle reaches the other side of the court quite gently. It also always flips to fly cork-first. The feathers act a little like those on an arrow, and much like the flight feathers that steady [[@how-birds-fly|birds]] in the air.

In 1980 Prakash Padukone became the first Indian to win the All England Championships, then the most important [[tournament|tournament]] in the sport. Pullela Gopichand won it in 2001 and later opened an academy in [[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]] that trained many of India's top players.

Saina Nehwal won India's first Olympic badminton medal, a bronze in London in 2012. [[@pv-sindhu|P. V. Sindhu]] won silver in Rio in 2016 and bronze in Tokyo, becoming one of India's most successful [[@olympics-india|Olympians]]. In 2022 India's men won the Thomas Cup, the world team championship, for the first time.

sec.h: A backyard game and an Olympic one
sec.t:
Badminton is the rare sport that works both in a garden with no lines and in a packed indoor arena. Across India and Asia, families play it on rooftops and streets in the evening, while in China, Indonesia, Denmark and Japan it is a major professional sport.

It joined the Olympics in 1992. Professional matches are played indoors, because the lightest breeze can push a shuttle off course. [[@sports-science|Sports scientists]] say top players can change direction hundreds of times in a single match, while most people in the crowd are just trying to follow the shuttle.

text: R.K. Laxman was one of India's best-loved cartoonists. Every day for more than half a century, he drew a small cartoon called *You Said It* on the front page of *The Times of India*. In a few lines of ink and one sentence of text, he made fun of politicians, potholes, power cuts and endless promises.

His most famous character was the Common Man: a short, balding man with glasses, a checked coat and a dhoti. He stood quietly at the side of the scene while important people talked. He stood for ordinary Indians who put up with whatever their leaders did next.

st.prompt: R.K. Laxman's Common Man appeared in cartoons for over 50 years. How much did he say?

options.t: Nothing at all. He only watched.
One short word in every cartoon
A long speech every Sunday

st.reveal: The Common Man almost never spoke. Others did the talking, usually politicians and officials making grand promises, while he stood in the corner looking puzzled or worried. Readers saw the joke through his eyes.

src: Laxman R.K. (1998) The Tunnel of Time (autobiography).
The Times of India, You Said It cartoon archive.

d.try: Draw a one-panel cartoon about something that happens at your school, like a long queue or a broken water cooler. Add one silent character in the corner who just watches. See whether a friend can understand the joke without any words from that character.
myth: Cartoons are only for children.

Newspaper cartoons are mostly made for adults. They poke fun at leaders and point out problems in a few lines. Laxman's cartoons were read every morning by millions of grown-ups, including the politicians he teased.
facts: You Said It, The Times of India, from 1951

sec.h: A boy who drew on the walls
sec.t:
Laxman grew up in Mysore, the youngest child in a large family that loved books. As a small boy he drew on walls, doors and floors: crows on a tree, his teachers, the neighbours. He later said that a British cartoonist in an old magazine, David Low, made him want to draw cartoons for a living.

When he applied to the J.J. School of Art in Bombay, he was rejected. He kept drawing anyway. He sent cartoons to newspapers, and drew pictures for the stories of his older brother, [[@rk-narayan|R.K. Narayan]], including the tales of the town of Malgudi.

A political cartoon works like a joke with a sting. It shows what a leader said next to what actually happened, and lets the reader notice the gap. In a [[@democracy-what|democracy]], that kind of teasing helps people question those in charge.

Laxman's cartoons were sharp but rarely cruel. He drew prime ministers for decades, starting with Jawaharlal [[@nehru|Nehru]]. During [[@emergency-1975|the Emergency]] of 1975 to 1977, when newspapers were censored, cartoonists had to be careful about what they printed.

He also created a cheerful mascot. In 1954 he drew Gattu, the paintbrush-holding boy used for years in advertisements for Asian Paints.

India has other famous cartoonists. K. Shankar Pillai, known as Shankar, started *Shankar's Weekly* in 1948 and later founded a [[@pop-barbie-dolls|dolls museum]] in Delhi. Mario Miranda filled his drawings of Goa with crowds of tiny, funny people. Pran created Chacha Chaudhary, whose brain is said to work faster than a computer, a favourite of [[@comics-india|Indian comics]] readers.

In the USA, Charles Schulz drew the *Peanuts* comic strip, with Charlie Brown and his dog Snoopy, for about 50 years, from 1950 to 2000. Like Laxman, he drew nearly every strip himself. Both men showed that a few lines on paper, repeated every day, can become part of a country's daily life.

text: [[vitamin|विटामिन]] ऐसे पदार्थ हैं जिनकी शरीर को ठीक से काम करने के लिए बहुत थोड़ी मात्रा में ज़रूरत होती है। ये प्रोटीन या कार्बोहाइड्रेट से कहीं कम चाहिए, अक्सर रोज़ बस एक ग्राम के कुछ हज़ारवें हिस्से जितने, पर इनके बिना गड़बड़ होने लगती है।

हर विटामिन के अपने काम हैं। विटामिन A मंद रोशनी में [[@eyes-see|आँखों को देखने]] में मदद करता है। विटामिन C उस मज़बूत [[protein|प्रोटीन]] को बनाने में मदद करता है जो त्वचा, मसूड़ों और खून की नलियों को जोड़े रखता है। विटामिन D [[@bones|हड्डियों]] को कैल्शियम लेने में मदद करता है। B विटामिन कोशिकाओं को खाने को ऊर्जा में बदलने में मदद करते हैं। शरीर ज़्यादातर विटामिन बना नहीं सकता, या काफ़ी नहीं बना सकता, इसलिए इन्हें खाने से आना पड़ता है। इंसानों को 13 विटामिन चाहिए।

sec.t:
1500 से 1700 के दशक तक लंबी समुद्री यात्राओं पर नाविकों को अक्सर स्कर्वी हो जाता था। उनके मसूड़ों से खून बहता, दाँत गिर जाते और पुराने घाव फिर से खुल जाते। [[@magellan|मैगलन की दुनिया भर की यात्रा]] पर भी बहुत-से नाविक इससे पीड़ित हुए।

1747 में स्कॉटलैंड के जहाज़ी डॉक्टर जेम्स लिंड ने एचएमएस सैलिसबरी नाम के जहाज़ पर एक प्रयोग किया। उन्होंने 12 बीमार नाविकों को जोड़ियों में बाँटा और हर जोड़ी को कुछ अलग दिया: सेब का रस, सिरका, समुद्र का पानी, संतरे और नींबू, और भी कुछ। जिस जोड़ी को [[@citrus|खट्टे फल]] मिले, वह तेज़ी से ठीक हो गई। इसमें दशकों लगे, पर 1790 के दशक तक ब्रिटिश नौसेना अपने नाविकों को नींबू का रस देने लगी। आज हम जानते हैं कि स्कर्वी विटामिन C की कमी से होता है।

विटामिन D अनोखा है। जब तुम्हारी [[@skin|त्वचा]] पर धूप पड़ती है, तो वह इसे बनाती है। इसकी कमी से बच्चों की हड्डियाँ नरम और टेढ़ी हो सकती हैं, जिस बीमारी को रिकेट्स, यानी सूखा रोग, कहते हैं। बहुत पहले यह ब्रिटेन और अमेरिका के धुएँ से भरे औद्योगिक शहरों में आम थी, जहाँ बच्चों को धूप कम मिलती थी। आज कई देशों में दूध में विटामिन D मिलाया जाता है।

तुम सोचोगे कि धूप वाले भारत में तो सबको भरपूर मिलता होगा। पर अध्ययनों में बहुत-से भारतीयों में विटामिन D कम पाया गया है, कुछ इसलिए कि लोग दिन का ज़्यादातर हिस्सा घर के अंदर बिताते हैं और गरमी से बचने के लिए खुद को ढके रहते हैं। रोज़ थोड़ी देर बाहर रहना मदद करता है।

ज़्यादातर लोगों को तरह-तरह के खाने से ही सारे ज़रूरी विटामिन मिल जाते हैं। [[@fruits-vegetables|फल और सब्ज़ियाँ]] इनमें से बहुत-से लाती हैं: आँवले, [[@guava-papaya|अमरूद]] और संतरे में विटामिन C, [[@food-why-carrots-orange|गाजर]], आम और हरी पत्तेदार सब्ज़ियों में विटामिन A। साबुत अनाज और दाल में B विटामिन होते हैं। विटामिन B12 ज़्यादातर दूध, दही और अंडे जैसी जानवरों से मिलने वाली चीज़ों से आता है, जो उन लोगों के लिए ध्यान देने की बात है जो जानवरों से मिलने वाली कोई भी चीज़ नहीं खाते।

कुछ विटामिन बहुत बड़ी खुराक में नुकसान कर सकते हैं, ख़ासकर A और D, जो शरीर की चर्बी और [[@liver|लिवर]] में जमा होते जाते हैं। इसीलिए विटामिन की गोलियाँ तभी लेनी चाहिए जब डॉक्टर या माता-पिता कहें। दुनिया भर में बच्चों का जो अंधापन रोका जा सकता है, उसकी एक बड़ी वजह आज भी विटामिन A की कमी है। इसे रोकने के लिए बहुत-से देश बच्चों को विटामिन A की ख़ुराक देते हैं।

text: Safety glass was discovered by accident in 1903 by the French chemist Édouard Bénédictus. He dropped a glass flask in his lab. It cracked into a spider web of lines, but the pieces stayed together in the flask's shape.

When he looked closer, he found the flask had once held [[cellulose|cellulose]] nitrate, a liquid that dries into a clear plastic film. That film was gripping the broken glass. Bénédictus realised that a sandwich of glass and plastic could stop sharp shards flying. He patented the idea in 1909. Today, car windscreens use the same trick.

It was made of very thick glass
It landed on something soft

st.reveal: The flask had held a liquid called cellulose nitrate, which dried into a thin, clear plastic film on the inside. When the glass cracked, the film stuck to the pieces and held them in place.

sec.t:
Ordinary glass, the kind in old windows and picture frames, breaks into long, knife-sharp pieces. In the early 1900s, as more cars took to the roads, crashes became a big problem. Windscreens made of normal glass caused terrible cuts.

Early cars often had no windscreen at all. Drivers wore goggles and long coats to keep out dust, rain and insects. Some cars reached speeds of 60 km/h or more, so a beetle in the eye was a real danger. When windscreens did arrive, they made driving more comfortable but crashes more dangerous.

Bénédictus called his product Triplex: glass, then plastic, then glass. At first it was expensive. Its first big use came in the First World War, for the eyepieces of soldiers' gas masks, where shattering glass could blind someone.

After the war, carmakers began to use laminated glass for windscreens. Early versions turned yellow or cloudy over time. In the 1930s, a tougher, clearer plastic called PVB replaced the old film, and laminated windscreens became standard. Today, in India, the USA and most countries, car windscreens must be made of laminated glass by law.

Laminated glass is a sandwich. When something hits it, the glass cracks but sticks to the plastic in the middle. It is used for windscreens, shop windows and glass floors on viewing platforms. Thick versions with many layers make bulletproof glass.

Toughened glass, also called tempered glass, works differently. It is heated to more than 600°C and then cooled very quickly with blasts of air. That locks tension inside the glass and makes it about four to five times stronger than normal glass. When it does break, it crumbles into thousands of small, blunt cubes. It is used in car side windows, oven doors and shower screens.

Safety glass keeps changing. Your phone screen is probably made from glass strengthened in a chemical bath, where small [[atom|atoms]] in the glass are swapped for bigger ones. These squeeze the surface and help it resist scratches and cracks, one of several tricks in [[@made-phone-screens|how phone screens are made]].

Safety glass also works alongside other inventions that protect people in cars. A cracked windscreen that stays in place helps hold people inside, while a [[@seatbelts|seatbelt]] and an [[@airbags|airbag]] stop bodies being thrown forward. Together, they have saved countless lives.

Bénédictus's dropped flask joins a long list of happy accidents. Another chemist, trying to make clear plastic for gun sights, got something so sticky it glued everything it touched, and that mistake became [[@accident-superglue|superglue]].

text: Phones run on lithium-ion [[@batteries|batteries]]. Inside, tiny charged particles called lithium ions shuttle between two layers. When you charge, they pack into one side, a layer of carbon called graphite. When you use the phone, they flow back to the other side, a metal oxide, and that flow pushes [[electron|electrons]] round the [[circuit|circuit]] to power the phone.

Each trip is a little imperfect. Some lithium gets stuck in side reactions and can never move again. The layers swell and shrink, and tiny cracks form. Over hundreds of charges, the battery can hold less and less. After about 500 to 1,000 full charges, many phone batteries keep only about 80% of what they could hold when new.

st.prompt: Which habit wears out a lithium-ion phone battery fastest?

options.t: Leaving it in a hot place while it's fully charged
Charging it before it reaches 0%
Unplugging it at 80%

st.reveal: Heat speeds up the unwanted chemical reactions inside the battery, and a full battery is under the most strain. Topping up before it runs flat is fine. Lithium-ion batteries actually prefer it.

myth: You should always let a phone battery run down to zero before charging, or it will "forget" its full size.
That was true of old nickel-cadmium batteries, which had a "memory effect". Lithium-ion batteries don't. Running them down to zero often actually wears them faster.

sec.t:
**Charge cycles.** One full cycle is using 100% of the battery, whether in one go or as two halves on different days. Every cycle adds a little wear.

**Heat.** Warmth speeds up the harmful reactions. A battery kept at 40°C ages much faster than one at room temperature. Phones left in hot cars or charging under a pillow suffer most.

**Being very full or very empty.** A battery sitting at 100% for hours is under strain, like a stretched rubber band. Draining to zero is hard on it too. Many phones now offer an "optimised charging" setting that holds at 80% overnight and finishes just before you wake.

**Fast charging.** Pushing energy in quickly makes heat. Phones slow down charging once they pass about 80% to protect the cells.

sec.h: Why your old phone dies at 20%
sec.t: As a battery ages, it also finds it harder to deliver a sudden burst of power. When you open a heavy game or the camera, the voltage dips. If it dips too low, the phone switches off to protect itself, even though the screen said there was charge left. Some phone makers slow down old phones slightly to avoid these surprise shutdowns.

The same chemistry powers laptops, e-scooters and [[@electric-cars|electric cars]]. Car makers wrap their batteries in cooling systems and stop drivers from using the very top and bottom of the charge, so the packs last many years. That's why an electric car can keep most of its range for well over 100,000 km.

Lithium is a soft, light metal, mined in places such as Australia, Chile and [[@argentina|Argentina]]. Phone batteries also contain cobalt, nickel or other [[mineral|minerals]], and some of these are mined in difficult conditions. That makes it worth keeping a battery healthy, and recycling it properly when it's finished. Throwing one in the bin is dangerous: a crushed lithium battery can catch fire in a rubbish truck, which is why old phones belong in [[@e-waste|e-waste]] collection.

sec.h: अपनी तारीफ़ ख़ुद लिखवाने वाले राजा
sec.t:
वंश के संस्थापक चंद्रगुप्त प्रथम लगभग 320 ईसवी में सत्ता में आए। उनके बेटे समुद्रगुप्त ने पूरे भारत में युद्ध अभियान चलाए। उनकी जीतों की तारीफ़ में एक लंबी कविता अशोक के एक पुराने स्तंभ पर खुदवाई गई, जो आज प्रयागराज में खड़ा है।

समुद्रगुप्त के कुछ सिक्कों पर वे [[@veena|वीणा]] जैसा तार वाला वाद्य बजाते दिखते हैं। कुछ पर बाघ का शिकार करते या घोड़े पर सवार। सोने के सिक्के छोटे-छोटे पोस्टरों जैसे थे, जो राजा की तस्वीर हर उस बाज़ार तक ले जाते जहाँ वे ख़र्च होते। उनके बेटे चंद्रगुप्त द्वितीय ने [[empire|साम्राज्य]] को पश्चिम में गुजरात तक फैलाया। उन्हें अक्सर किस्सों वाले राजा विक्रमादित्य से जोड़ा जाता है, जो अपनी बुद्धि और अपने दरबार के नवरत्नों के लिए मशहूर हैं।

sec.h: खंभा जिस पर ज़ंग नहीं लगता
sec.t:
[[@delhi|दिल्ली]] के क़ुतुब परिसर में लगभग 7 मीटर ऊँचा एक [[@mystery-iron-pillar|लौह स्तंभ]] खड़ा है, यानी किसी दो-मंज़िला घर जितना। इस पर खुदा [[inscription|अभिलेख]] चंद्र नाम के एक राजा की तारीफ़ करता है, जिन्हें आमतौर पर चंद्रगुप्त द्वितीय माना जाता है।

बाहर पड़ा मामूली लोहा कुछ ही सालों में नारंगी और भुरभुरा हो जाता है। यह खंभा लगभग 1,600 साल से खड़ा है और उस पर बस हल्का-सा [[@rust|ज़ंग]] है। वैज्ञानिकों ने पाया कि इसमें फ़ॉस्फ़ोरस ज़्यादा होने से इसकी सतह पर एक पतली रक्षा-परत बन जाती है। उस ज़माने में लोहे का इतना बड़ा एक ही टुकड़ा गढ़ना बहुत बड़ी बात थी।

कालिदास का नाटक *अभिज्ञानशाकुंतलम्* एक ऐसे राजा की कहानी है जो एक शाप की वजह से अपनी प्रेमिका को भूल जाता है। 1789 में इसका अंग्रेज़ी अनुवाद हुआ, और बाद में जर्मन कवि गेटे इसे पढ़कर झूम उठे।

आज के इतिहासकार ज़्यादा कड़े सवाल पूछते हैं। ज़्यादातर लोग किसान थे, जो कर चुकाते थे और सोने का सिक्का शायद ही कभी देखते थे। [[@caste-history|जाति]] के नियम और कड़े हो गए, और कुछ समूहों को समाज से बाहर माना जाने लगा।

400 के दशक के आख़िर से मध्य एशिया के हूण कहे जाने वाले समूहों के हमलों ने साम्राज्य को कमज़ोर किया, और लगभग 550 ईसवी तक यह बिखर गया। इसलिए कला और विज्ञान में यह दौर ख़ूब चमकता है, जबकि बहुत से लोगों की रोज़ की ज़िंदगी उतनी सुनहरी नहीं थी।

text: No one lives in Antarctica permanently. There are no towns, no farms and no native people. Instead, about 70 research stations run by around 30 countries dot the continent, mostly near the coast.

In the short summer, a few thousand [[@antarctica-stations|scientists]], engineers, cooks, doctors and pilots live and work there. In winter, when the Sun doesn't rise for weeks and it is too stormy for most planes to land, about a thousand people stay behind. They study ice, weather, rocks, animals and space, then go home after a few months or a year. The only permanent residents are [[@penguin-flight|penguins]], seals and a few hardy insects and mosses.

sec.t:
Antarctica holds the [[@weather-records|world record for cold]]. On 21 July 1983, Russia's Vostok Station measured minus 89.2 °C, colder than the inside of a home freezer by about 70 degrees. Winds rushing down from the high ice can blow faster than a speeding car.

Strangely, Antarctica is also a [[@deserts-world|desert]]. Very little snow falls each year in the interior, but because it almost never melts, it piles up over hundreds of thousands of years. That has built an ice sheet so heavy it pushes the rock beneath below sea level.

In 1959, twelve countries signed the Antarctic Treaty. It says Antarctica may be used only for peaceful purposes and science. Military bases and weapons tests are banned, and scientists are expected to share what they find. A later agreement, the Madrid Protocol of 1991, banned mining too. Today over 50 countries have signed it.

The United States runs the largest station, McMurdo, which can hold over a thousand people in summer. It has a harbour, an airstrip, a fire station and even a coffee shop. The US also runs the Amundsen-Scott station at the South Pole itself, named after the two explorers who raced there in 1911 and 1912, a story you can read in [[@explorers-poles|polar explorers]].

Daily life can feel like living on a spaceship. People share small rooms, eat together, and take turns washing dishes. Fresh fruit and vegetables run out in winter, so some stations grow salad in greenhouses under lamps.

Going outside means layers of thermal clothing, goggles and checking in by radio. People celebrate midwinter in June with special dinners and greetings sent between stations from different countries.

The ice is a record of the past. Snow that fell long ago traps tiny bubbles of air, and as more snow piles on top, those bubbles are sealed in. Scientists drill out long cylinders of ice, called cores, and read the air from hundreds of thousands of years ago, as explained in [[@ice-ages|ice ages]].

This matters for the future too. [[@what-if-ice-melted|If all of Antarctica's ice melted]], which would take a very long time, seas would rise by tens of metres.

text: The United Kingdom, or UK, is a country in north-west Europe made up of four countries: England, [[@scotland|Scotland]], Wales and Northern Ireland. They share one king, one army, one [[currency|currency]] (the pound) and one main [[parliament|parliament]] in London.

Each also has its own identity. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have their own parliaments or assemblies that make many decisions about schools, hospitals and local laws. Each has its own flag, its own patron saint and, often, its own sports teams. People may call themselves Scottish or Welsh first, and British second.

sec.t:
The names can be confusing. Great Britain is the biggest island, holding England, Scotland and Wales. Ireland is the island to its west. Most of Ireland is a separate country, the Republic of Ireland, while the north-eastern part, Northern Ireland, belongs to the UK. The British Isles is a geographical name for all these islands together, though many people in Ireland dislike it.

There are smaller places too. The Isle of Man and the Channel Islands, such as Jersey, belong to the British Crown but are not officially part of the UK. They make most of their own laws.

Scotland has its own legal system, its own banknotes and Gaelic, along with mountains called the Highlands. Edinburgh's castle stands on top of an [[extinct|extinct]] volcano. Wales has its own language, Welsh, which more than half a million people speak. Road signs there are written in both Welsh and English.

Northern Ireland has the [[@earth-weird-giants-causeway|Giant's Causeway]], a coast of about 40,000 six-sided stone columns made by cooling [[lava|lava]]. Its recent history includes a long conflict known as the Troubles, which largely ended with the Good Friday Agreement in 1998. England is the largest country by far, with London, the capital of the UK.

In [[@football-world|football]], England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each play as separate national teams. England and Scotland played the first international match in 1872. In rugby, Northern Ireland's players join the Republic's in a single team for the whole island of Ireland. In cricket, the England team represents both England and Wales, and plays some of the oldest [[@test-cricket|Test cricket]] rivalries in the world.

At the Olympics, though, all four compete together as one team, Great Britain. So a Welsh cyclist and a Scottish swimmer may be rivals in one sport and teammates in another.

The [[@east-india-company|East India Company]], founded in London in 1600, began as a trading business and ended up ruling much of India. The British government took over direct rule in 1858, which lasted until India's independence in 1947. That long, often painful history explains why English is so widely spoken in India, and why cricket is so loved.

Today about 1.8 million people of Indian heritage live in the UK, one of its largest communities. Chicken tikka masala is often listed among Britain's favourite dishes. Many words travelled the other way too. English took "shampoo", "bungalow" and "pyjamas" from Indian languages, and the plays of [[@shakespeare|Shakespeare]] are now performed in Hindi, Bengali and Tamil.

text: An encyclopedia tries to gather what is known about many subjects in one place, arranged so you can find things. For most of history this was done by hand. Teams of scholars wrote, copied and checked thousands of entries, then sorted them by topic or alphabet. Printing made it possible to sell copies widely. Computers and the internet changed it again.

The idea is very old. Ancient Romans, Chinese emperors, Arab scholars and Indian kings all made collections of knowledge. The modern word comes from Greek words meaning something like "all-round learning".

sec.t:
Around 77 CE, a Roman officer called Pliny the Elder finished his *Natural History* in 37 books. He said it held 20,000 facts drawn from about 2,000 books. It covered stars, animals, plants, metals and medicines.

Some of it was wrong. Pliny believed in people with one giant foot they used as a sunshade. But it was copied for over a thousand years. Pliny commanded a fleet near Naples, and in 79 CE he sailed towards Mount Vesuvius during the eruption that buried [[@pompeii|Pompeii]]. He died on the shore.

In 1403 the Chinese emperor Yongle ordered scholars to collect all knowledge into one work. By 1408 more than 2,000 people had produced the Yongle Encyclopedia: 11,095 handwritten volumes. Only the original and one later copy were ever made, because it was far too big to print.

Wars and fires destroyed most of it. Today only about 400 volumes survive, scattered across libraries in China, Europe and the USA.

Its makers did not write new essays. They copied whole books and passages from older works, sorted under topics. Because of that, the surviving volumes preserve pieces of books that are otherwise lost.

{{story:great-libraries}}

In India, the Western [[@chalukyas|Chalukya]] king Someshvara III wrote the *Manasollasa* in Sanskrit in about 1129. It is often called an encyclopedia. It covers ruling a kingdom, cooking, music, painting, horses, elephants, games and even how to enjoy a garden.

It is one of the best records of what people ate in [[medieval|medieval]] south India, including recipes for dishes that sound like early versions of idli and dosa.

In France in the 1750s, Denis Diderot and Jean d'Alembert published the *Encyclopédie* in 28 volumes, with beautiful drawings of machines and crafts. Its ideas annoyed the king and the church, and it was banned more than once.

In Edinburgh, [[@scotland|Scotland]], the *Encyclopaedia Britannica* first came out in weekly parts from 1768 to 1771. It grew with each edition. Later editions invited well-known experts to write long articles. The famous 11th edition of 1910–11 had articles by scientists and explorers of the day, and some readers still collect it. By its last printing it filled 32 heavy volumes and took up a whole shelf. The last printed edition came out in 2010. Since then, Britannica has been published online.

In 2001 Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger started [[@wikipedia-how|Wikipedia]], an online encyclopedia anyone can edit. The English version passed 6 million articles in 2020. Volunteers check each other's work and argue on discussion pages about what counts as a reliable source. Wikipedia now exists in more than 300 languages, including Hindi, Tamil, Bengali and Santali.

Encyclopedias have always had to balance speed and accuracy. Printed ones were slow to update. Online ones can change in minutes, for better or worse. The best ones, old and new, show where each fact comes from.

text: Langston Hughes was an American poet and writer, and one of the leading voices of the Harlem Renaissance. That was a burst of Black art, music and writing in the Harlem neighbourhood of New York in the 1920s and 1930s.

He wrote about ordinary Black Americans: cooks, lift operators, students and musicians. He wanted his poems to sound like the people he knew, so he borrowed the [[rhythm|rhythms]] of [[@jazz|jazz]] and the [[@blues|blues]]. His poems are short, clear and musical, which is why children in American schools still read them aloud.

sec.h: A boy who moved a lot
sec.t:
Hughes was born in Joplin, Missouri, in 1901. His parents separated, and he spent much of his childhood with his grandmother in Lawrence, Kansas. She told him stories about the fight against slavery, and he read everything he could find. Books, he later wrote, became a place to escape to.

At grammar school in Lincoln, Illinois, his classmates elected him class poet. In his memoir he says they assumed a Black boy must have rhythm. Later, at high school in Cleveland, Ohio, he wrote for the school magazine and began to take poetry seriously.

In 1925 Hughes was working as a busboy, clearing tables, at a hotel in Washington DC. The well-known poet Vachel Lindsay was dining there. Hughes slipped three of his poems beside Lindsay's plate. That evening Lindsay read them to an audience and told them he had found a new poet. Newspapers picked up the story. Hughes had left Columbia University a few years earlier, unhappy with the racism he met there. Now he went back to studying, at Lincoln University in Pennsylvania.

The next year Hughes published his first book, *The Weary Blues*. Some Black critics thought he made Black life look rough by writing about clubs and working people. Hughes answered that he wanted to show people as they really were.

His poem "I, Too" ends with a Black man who is sent to eat in the kitchen, but says one day he will sit at the table. It is a quiet, confident poem about belonging in America. "Harlem" (1951) asks what happens to "a dream deferred". Lorraine Hansberry took a line from it for her play *A Raisin in the Sun*.

Hughes travelled widely, to Africa, Europe, the Soviet Union and Japan. In the 1950s he was questioned by a US Senate committee about his left-wing poems from the 1930s, a hard time for many American writers.

Hughes lived for about twenty years in a brownstone house on East 127th Street in Harlem, now a protected landmark. He died in 1967. His ashes rest under the floor of the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, part of the New York Public Library. The floor there has a design based on "The Negro Speaks of Rivers", so visitors walk over his poem.

text: In the kitchen, a berry is any small, soft, juicy fruit. By that rule a strawberry is a berry.

But scientists who study plants, called [[botanist|botanists]], use the word in a stricter way. To them, a true berry is a fleshy fruit that grows from a single flower with one ovary, the part that holds the seeds. It usually has several seeds inside the flesh, and the whole wall of the fruit is soft.

By that rule a strawberry is not a berry. Its seeds are on the outside, and the juicy red part grows from a different bit of the flower. Meanwhile bananas, tomatoes, grapes, guavas, brinjals and chillies all pass the test.

sec.t:
Long before botany, people called small soft fruits "berries". The English word goes back over a thousand years. When scientists began sorting fruits by how they grow, they borrowed the word and gave it a tighter meaning.

So both are right, in their own place. A cook calling a strawberry a berry isn't wrong. A botanist saying it isn't one isn't wrong either. They are just using the word in different ways, as people often do with [[@words-borrowed|borrowed words]].

sec.h: Why a strawberry isn't a berry
sec.t:
Look at a strawberry flower. In the middle is a little raised cushion with lots of tiny ovaries on it. After the flower is [[@pollinators|pollinated]], each ovary turns into a small, hard, dry fruit, with one seed inside. Those are the "seeds" you see on the outside of a strawberry. Botanists call them achenes.

The red, juicy part we eat isn't really fruit at all. It is the swollen cushion of the flower that held them up. So a strawberry is a cluster of about 200 tiny fruits sitting on a sweet, fleshy base.

Strawberries are also in the rose family, along with apples, pears and almonds. Raspberries and mulberries are different again. Each one is a bundle of many tiny juicy fruits stuck together, which is why they look bumpy.

{{story:seeds-fly}}

A [[@bananas|banana]] grows from one flower ovary, with soft flesh all through and tiny seeds in the middle. Those black specks are the seeds of the wild banana, shrunk almost to nothing in the kinds we eat. So a banana is a true berry.

[[@tomatoes|Tomatoes]], chillies and brinjals belong to the same plant family, and they are berries too. So are grapes, blueberries, kiwi fruit, guavas and jamun.

Some fruits are close relatives of berries with a tougher skin. Pumpkins, cucumbers and watermelons have a hard rind, and botanists give them their own name, pepo. Lemons and oranges are another special kind of berry, called a hesperidium, with a leathery peel and juicy segments.

The large garden strawberry we eat today is quite young. It was first bred in France in the 1700s by crossing two wild [[species|species]], one from North America and one from Chile.

In India, the town of Mahabaleshwar, high in the hills of Maharashtra, is famous for strawberries. Cool winters suit them, and families visit to pick them fresh, make jam and drink strawberry milkshakes. Farmers in parts of Himachal Pradesh and the northeast grow them too. India also has its own berry stars, like the purple jamun that stains your tongue in early summer.

In the USA, California grows most of the country's strawberries. Blueberries and cranberries are native to North America. Cranberries are often harvested by flooding their fields, so the ripe red berries float to the surface, where farmers scoop them up.

Ask a friend to hand you a berry, and the botanist's answer might be a banana.

text: पनीर बनाने के लिए [[@food-science-milk-boil|दूध को उबाला जाता है]] और उसमें [[@citrus|नींबू का रस]] या सिरका निचोड़ दिया जाता है। लगभग फ़ौरन दूध फट जाता है। उसमें नरम सफ़ेद थक्के बन जाते हैं, और वे एक पतले हरे-पीले पानी में तैरने लगते हैं। इस पानी को व्हे कहते हैं।

इन थक्कों को मलमल के कपड़े में डालकर धोया और निचोड़ा जाता है। फिर ऊपर कोई भारी चीज़, जैसे पानी से भरा पतीला, घंटे भर के लिए रख दिया जाता है, ताकि वे दबकर एक ठोस टुकड़ा बन जाएँ। यही पनीर है। इसे न तो महीनों रखकर पकाना पड़ता है, न किसी ख़ास फफूँद की ज़रूरत होती है, न रेनेट की। इसीलिए घर में उसी दिन ताज़ा पनीर बन जाता है।

sec.t:
दूध में केसीन नाम का एक [[protein|प्रोटीन]] भरा होता है। आम तौर पर केसीन नन्हे-नन्हे गुच्छों में तैरता रहता है, और ये गुच्छे एक-दूसरे को दूर धकेलते हैं, कुछ वैसे ही जैसे दो चुंबकों को उलटी तरफ़ से पास लाओ तो वे भागते हैं।

[[acid|अम्ल]], यानी खटाई, यह खेल बदल देता है। वह उस [[charge|आवेश]] को ख़त्म कर देता है जो गुच्छों को अलग रखता था। अब गुच्छे आपस में टकराकर चिपकने लगते हैं। गर्मी इस काम को और तेज़ कर देती है। दूध की चिकनाई इन थक्कों के अंदर फँस जाती है। पानी, दूध की शक्कर [[lactose|लैक्टोज़]] और कुछ दूसरे प्रोटीन के साथ व्हे बनकर बह जाता है। बहुत-से लोग इस पानी से रोटी का आटा गूँधते हैं या दाल पकाते हैं, ताकि कुछ भी बेकार न जाए।

पुराने भारतीय ग्रंथों में दूध से बनी बहुत-सी चीज़ों का ज़िक्र है, जैसे दही, मक्खन, घी और खोया। पर खटाई से दूध फाड़कर बनाई गई चीज़ का साफ़ ज़िक्र कम मिलता है। लगता है कि कुछ प्राचीन लेखक जान-बूझकर दूध फाड़ने को ठीक नहीं मानते थे।

खाने के इतिहासकार के.टी. अचाया का मानना था कि 1600 के दशक में बंगाल में बसे पुर्तगालियों ने शायद वहाँ के रसोइयों को खटाई से दूध फाड़ना सिखाया, और इसी से छेना बना। "पनीर" शब्द फ़ारसी से आया है, जहाँ *पनीर* का मतलब बस चीज़ है। इसलिए कुछ इतिहासकार पनीर को फ़ारस और अफ़ग़ानिस्तान के रसोइयों से जोड़ते हैं। हो सकता है दोनों बातें थोड़ी-थोड़ी सच हों। जानकार आज भी इस पर एकमत नहीं हैं।

पनीर चीज़ की सबसे सीधी-सादी किस्मों में से एक है। दुनिया के ज़्यादातर दूसरे चीज़, जैसे चेडर या मोत्ज़ारेला, रेनेट से जमाए जाते हैं। रेनेट में एक [[enzyme|एंज़ाइम]] होता है जो केसीन को काट-छाँटकर जेली जैसा बना देता है। स्वाद के लिए इसमें मददगार [[bacteria|बैक्टीरिया]] मिलाए जाते हैं। फिर ज़्यादातर चीज़ में नमक डालकर उन्हें आकार दिया जाता है और हफ़्तों या सालों तक पकने के लिए रख दिया जाता है।

इंसान बहुत लंबे समय से चीज़ बना रहे हैं। वैज्ञानिकों को पोलैंड में मिट्टी की छलनियों पर दूध की चिकनाई के निशान मिले, जो लगभग 7,000 साल पहले इस्तेमाल होती थीं, शायद चीज़ बनाने के लिए। 2018 में शोधकर्ताओं ने बताया कि मिस्र की एक क़ब्र में उन्हें 3,000 साल से भी पुराना चीज़ का एक टुकड़ा मिला है। इसके बारे में [[@ancient-egypt|प्राचीन मिस्र]] में पढ़ो।

अमेरिका दुनिया में सबसे ज़्यादा चीज़ बनाता है। वहाँ का विस्कॉन्सिन राज्य चेडर चीज़ के लिए मशहूर है, और वहाँ की फ़ुटबॉल टीम के प्रशंसक चीज़ के टुकड़े जैसी फ़ोम की "चीज़हेड" टोपियाँ पहनकर मैच देखने आते हैं। अब अमेरिका भर में भारतीय किराना दुकानों पर पनीर के टुकड़े बिकते हैं, और कुछ अमेरिकी डेयरियाँ भी पनीर बनाने लगी हैं।

पनीर में प्रोटीन भी ख़ूब होता है। जिस देश में बहुत-से लोग शाकाहारी हों, वहाँ यह बड़ी बात है। मटर पनीर की एक प्लेट बिना मांस के खाने को पेट भरने वाला बनाने का सबसे आसान तरीक़ा है।
